A fast Fourier transform computes the same result more efficiently; it does not provide a different frequency definition or repair incorrect sampling. A useful implementation should specify sign, normalization, input length, and the mapping from bins to physical frequencies. Without those conventions, two numerically plausible arrays can represent different transforms.

entry.title: Cryptographic Algorithms in Swift: SHA-256, X25519, and Derived Keys

link.title: Cryptographic Algorithms in Swift: SHA-256, X25519, and Derived Keys

entry.content:
Hashing, key agreement, key derivation, and authenticated encryption solve different problems. SHA-256 produces a deterministic digest. Diffie-Hellman-style agreement lets two private-key holders derive shared secret material. Neither operation by itself authenticates a remote person’s identity or encrypts an application message.

A useful Swift treatment connects the mathematics to established APIs and makes those boundaries explicit, rather than presenting toy modular arithmetic as a deployable protocol.

The examples use Swift 5.7 syntax and Apple’s CryptoKit, introduced in 2019. X25519 is specified in RFC 7748. The local two-party demonstration is not a complete network handshake.

SHA-256 commits to bytes, not an abstract object

import Foundation
import CryptoKit

let message = Data("abc".utf8)
let hash = SHA256.hash(data: message)
let hexadecimal = hash.map { String(format: "%02x", Int($0)) }.joined()
assert(hexadecimal == "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad")
assert(SHA256.hash(data: message) == hash)

The encoding is explicit UTF-8. Hashing a record requires a canonical byte serialization: field order, integer endianness, string normalization, and schema version all matter.

For B input bytes, hashing takes linear processing work while the SHA-256 digest remains 32 bytes. A streaming hash can process chunks without retaining the entire message. Constant output size is not constant input-processing time.

A digest is not encryption and has no decryption key. A plain hash also does not authenticate who supplied the message. For shared-key message authentication, use an established MAC such as HMAC through its API, not a homemade concatenation construction.

Security properties have different work factors

For an ideal b-bit hash, generic preimage search has work on the scale of 2ᵇ, while collision search has birthday-scale work around 2^(b/2). These are idealized attack-cost models, not runtime benchmarks of this program.

\[P(\text{collision among }q\text{ random digests})\approx 1-e^{-q(q-1)/2^{b+1}}.\]

A small hash table deliberately tolerates collisions and resolves equality afterward. A cryptographic commitment instead depends on collisions being infeasible to find. Swift’s randomized Hasher serves the former purpose and is not a substitute for SHA-256.

Password storage is another problem. Fast hashing makes bulk password guesses cheap. Use a dedicated password-hashing design with appropriate work and memory factors; do not treat the digest example as a password database recipe.

Diffie-Hellman establishes shared material

Classical finite-field notation writes public values as A = gᵃ mod p and B = gᵇ mod p, with both sides deriving gᵃᵇ mod p. X25519 uses a specified elliptic-curve operation instead of that toy representation.

CryptoKit generates private keys and performs the operation:

let alice = Curve25519.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey()
let bob = Curve25519.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey()
let aliceSecret = try alice.sharedSecretFromKeyAgreement(with: bob.publicKey)
let bobSecret = try bob.sharedSecretFromKeyAgreement(with: alice.publicKey)

let context = Data("example-v1/client-to-server".utf8) +
    alice.publicKey.rawRepresentation + bob.publicKey.rawRepresentation
let salt = Data("public example session salt".utf8)
let aliceKey = aliceSecret.hkdfDerivedSymmetricKey(
    using: SHA256.self, salt: salt, sharedInfo: context, outputByteCount: 32
)
let bobKey = bobSecret.hkdfDerivedSymmetricKey(
    using: SHA256.self, salt: salt, sharedInfo: context, outputByteCount: 32
)
let aliceBytes = aliceKey.withUnsafeBytes { Data($0) }
let bobBytes = bobKey.withUnsafeBytes { Data($0) }
assert(aliceBytes == bobBytes)

The equality check is a local test and does not print secret bytes. Application logs should not retain private keys, shared secrets, or derived keys.

HKDF turns shared material into a purpose-specific symmetric key. Its context binds the demonstrated role and public-key ordering. A reverse-direction key should use a distinct context rather than reuse this label indiscriminately.

The salt need not be secret. A real protocol defines how it is selected and authenticated, along with the exact transcript and encoding. The fixed text here keeps the local example reproducible in structure while fresh private keys still vary each run.

Authenticate the public-key exchange

An attacker who substitutes public keys can establish a different shared key with each endpoint. Both local agreement operations may succeed while the endpoints are communicating through the attacker.

A complete protocol authenticates peers or their key exchange through a trusted mechanism, such as validated certificates or pinned signing keys. Including exchanged keys in HKDF context binds bytes into derivation but does not establish whose keys they are.

Prefer established secure transport or protocol implementations for network features. This article’s purpose is to understand the primitives’ roles and test their composition locally.

Use authenticated encryption for message bytes

let plaintext = Data("delivery instructions".utf8)
let sealed = try AES.GCM.seal(plaintext, using: aliceKey, authenticating: context)
let opened = try AES.GCM.open(sealed, using: bobKey, authenticating: context)
assert(opened == plaintext)

var tampered = Array(sealed.combined!)
tampered[tampered.count - 1] ^= 1
do {
    let altered = try AES.GCM.SealedBox(combined: Data(tampered))
    _ = try AES.GCM.open(altered, using: bobKey, authenticating: context)
    assertionFailure("Modified authenticated ciphertext must fail")
} catch {
    // Expected: the altered tag or ciphertext is rejected.
}

The default seal operation generates its nonce. Nonce reuse under one GCM key is dangerous; do not replace generation with a counter or constant without a complete uniqueness and lifecycle design.

The combined representation is available for this standard nonce size. A production decoder should handle malformed containers as errors rather than force-unwrapping untrusted input.

Authenticated additional data is checked but not encrypted. It can bind version, direction, or record metadata to the ciphertext. Both parties must use the identical bytes.

Test vectors and negative tests serve different purposes

The SHA-256 vector checks a known deterministic output. Random key agreement checks both parties derive compatible keys. Tampering, wrong associated data, wrong peer keys, and malformed public-key bytes test rejection behavior.

These tests do not prove side-channel resistance or protocol security. The established primitive implementation supplies properties that should not be reimplemented in ordinary Swift loops with data-dependent secret branching.

Resource limits matter at the parser boundary too: validate message lengths and formats before allocating huge buffers. Keep cryptographic failures distinct from successful empty plaintext.

Derive separate keys for separate purposes

let reverseContext = Data("example-v1/server-to-client".utf8) +
    alice.publicKey.rawRepresentation + bob.publicKey.rawRepresentation
let reverseKey = aliceSecret.hkdfDerivedSymmetricKey(
    using: SHA256.self, salt: salt, sharedInfo: reverseContext, outputByteCount: 32
)
let reverseBytes = reverseKey.withUnsafeBytes { Data($0) }
assert(reverseBytes != aliceBytes)
do {
    _ = try AES.GCM.open(sealed, using: bobKey, authenticating: reverseContext)
    assertionFailure("A different context must not authenticate this record")
} catch {}

Distinct derivation labels separate traffic directions, while authenticated data binds a particular record to its context. These mechanisms are complementary rather than interchangeable.

A protocol also needs record sequence numbers or another replay policy. Successfully authenticating a previously valid ciphertext does not prove it is fresh. Replaying the same message can be harmful even when no cryptographic bit has been altered.

Public-key encoding is an input boundary

Received key bytes should be decoded through the established public-key initializer and failures handled before key agreement. Do not accept an arbitrary byte array as a key merely because its length looks plausible.

The wire format should identify the protocol and algorithm version unambiguously. Negotiation itself must be authenticated against downgrade behavior in a complete design.

This is why local agreement and encryption snippets are best understood as primitive tests. They demonstrate compatibility and rejection behavior within a fixed context, while a deployed channel additionally defines identities, freshness, negotiation, lifetime, and recovery.

Hash a stream without changing its byte identity

var incremental = SHA256()
incremental.update(data: Data("a".utf8))
incremental.update(data: Data("bc".utf8))
assert(incremental.finalize() == hash)

Chunk boundaries do not change the digest of the same concatenated bytes. That permits a file reader to feed bounded buffers rather than load an entire file into memory.

The reader still needs failure handling. A digest calculated from a truncated stream is a valid digest of the truncated bytes, not evidence that the intended full file was read. Preserve expected length or an authenticated manifest when completeness matters.

Do not compare a partially calculated digest with an expected value until all reads have succeeded. A resource-efficient implementation and a trustworthy integrity workflow are separate properties.

Exercise: bind direction and version

Derive a second key using a server-to-client label and verify its bytes differ from the first. Test opening a message with the wrong direction key and wrong associated data. Explain which facts those failures establish and why they still do not authenticate an unauthenticated public-key exchange.

See Apple’s CryptoKit documentation for the supported primitive APIs.

A useful Swift treatment connects the mathematics to established APIs and makes those boundaries explicit, rather than presenting toy modular arithmetic as a deployable protocol.

entry.title: Three-Tier Architecture in Swift: Presentation, Use Cases, and Data Boundaries

link.title: Three-Tier Architecture in Swift: Presentation, Use Cases, and Data Boundaries

entry.content:
Three-tier architecture separates presentation, application behavior, and data management. Those responsibilities can be deployed as client, application server, and database, while their source-code boundaries still need explicit dependency contracts.

Merely creating three folders does not produce a useful architecture. The important question is which layer owns validation, domain decisions, persistence guarantees, and translation of failures.

The Swift 5.7 case study implements a library-loan workflow in one process so its responsibilities can be tested. A physically separated three-tier deployment adds network, authentication, serialization, and operational concerns beyond this local example.

Put use-case rules in the application tier

struct LoanRequest { let bookID: Int; let memberID: Int; let days: Int }
struct LoanReceipt: Equatable { let bookID: Int; let memberID: Int; let dueDay: Int }
enum LoanFailure: Error {
    case invalidRequest
    case inactiveMember
    case unavailableBook
    case storageUnavailable
}

protocol LoanStoring {
    func createLoan(bookID: Int, memberID: Int, dueDay: Int) throws -> LoanReceipt
}

struct LoanService {
    let store: any LoanStoring
    func borrow(_ request: LoanRequest, today: Int) throws -> LoanReceipt {
        guard request.bookID > 0, request.memberID > 0, today >= 0,
              (1...14).contains(request.days) else { throw LoanFailure.invalidRequest }
        let due = today.addingReportingOverflow(request.days)
        guard !due.overflow else { throw LoanFailure.invalidRequest }
        return try store.createLoan(bookID: request.bookID, memberID: request.memberID,
                                    dueDay: due.partialValue)
    }
}

The service owns the supported loan duration and calculation. It depends on an application-facing persistence capability, not a database connection or query object.

today is a supplied day number. A boundary adapter must define the calendar and time zone when translating real timestamps into this model. The domain calculation should not read a hidden system clock halfway through the workflow.

Give the data boundary an atomic contract

final class MemoryLoanStore: LoanStoring {
    private var available: [Int: Int]
    private let activeMembers: Set<Int>
    private(set) var loans: [LoanReceipt] = []
    init(available: [Int: Int], activeMembers: Set<Int>) {
        precondition(available.values.allSatisfy { $0 >= 0 })
        self.available = available
        self.activeMembers = activeMembers
    }
    func createLoan(bookID: Int, memberID: Int, dueDay: Int) throws -> LoanReceipt {
        guard activeMembers.contains(memberID) else { throw LoanFailure.inactiveMember }
        guard let count = available[bookID], count > 0 else { throw LoanFailure.unavailableBook }
        let receipt = LoanReceipt(bookID: bookID, memberID: memberID, dueDay: dueDay)
        available[bookID] = count - 1
        loans.append(receipt)
        return receipt
    }
}

This in-memory adapter requires serialized access. Within one call it checks member status and inventory before changing stock and recording the loan. A production database adapter needs a transaction or equivalent atomic operation preserving those relationships under concurrent borrowers.

Exposing separate hasCopy, decrementCopy, and insertLoan calls would force the service to orchestrate a race-prone check-then-write sequence. A narrow domain operation can express the persistence guarantee the use case actually needs.

If membership lives in another external system, the guarantee needs a cross-system policy rather than a claim that one local transaction covers everything.

Keep presentation parsing and result mapping separate

enum BorrowViewState: Equatable {
    case invalidInput
    case success(LoanReceipt)
    case inactiveMember
    case unavailableBook
    case unavailable
}

struct BorrowPresenter {
    let service: LoanService
    func submit(book: String, member: String, days: String, today: Int) -> BorrowViewState {
        guard let bookID = Int(book), let memberID = Int(member), let duration = Int(days) else {
            return .invalidInput
        }
        do {
            let receipt = try service.borrow(LoanRequest(bookID: bookID, memberID: memberID,
                                                         days: duration), today: today)
            return .success(receipt)
        } catch LoanFailure.invalidRequest { return .invalidInput }
        catch LoanFailure.inactiveMember { return .inactiveMember }
        catch LoanFailure.unavailableBook { return .unavailableBook }
        catch { return .unavailable }
    }
}

let store = MemoryLoanStore(available: [7: 1], activeMembers: [3])
let service = LoanService(store: store)
let presenter = BorrowPresenter(service: service)
assert(presenter.submit(book: "7", member: "3", days: "30", today: 100) == .invalidInput)
assert(store.loans.isEmpty)
assert(presenter.submit(book: "7", member: "3", days: "14", today: 100) ==
       .success(LoanReceipt(bookID: 7, memberID: 3, dueDay: 114)))
assert(presenter.submit(book: "7", member: "3", days: "14", today: 100) == .unavailableBook)
assert(store.loans.count == 1)

The presenter translates text into a request and maps domain outcomes into display state. It does not know how inventory is stored or repeat the fourteen-day rule in its own branch.

The service still validates parsed values because other callers may bypass this presenter. Presentation validation improves feedback; it is not the only enforcement of a domain invariant.

Distinguish runtime flow from source dependencies

flowchart LR
    accTitle: A three-tier request crosses presentation, application, and data responsibilities
    Presentation[Presentation: parse input and display outcomes] --> Application[Application: loan policy and use case]
    Application --> Data[Data: atomic loan persistence]
    Data --> Receipt[Domain receipt or failure]
    Receipt --> Presentation

At runtime, the service invokes the store. In source code, the application owns LoanStoring, and a data adapter implements that contract. This keeps domain policy from importing a particular persistence SDK.

A physically deployed application server and database introduce network boundaries. The Swift client should not gain direct database credentials merely because the local tutorial uses one process.

Put guarantees where they can be enforced

The application tier defines what a valid loan means. The data tier enforces stock consistency and atomic recording under concurrency. The presentation tier explains outcomes to the user.

If all validation exists only in UI controls, a background import can bypass it. If every domain rule is hardcoded in a screen’s database query, another client can implement a different policy. If storage exposes no conditional operation, a service cannot invent atomicity from separate calls.

Use contracts that match the required guarantee, then test each boundary and the assembled use case.

Failure and retries cross tiers too

A timeout between application server and client can happen after the loan committed. Blindly resubmitting may create another loan if stock remains. A request identity and durable idempotency protocol can make retries safe under the chosen scope.

Mapping every failure to “book unavailable” hides infrastructure outages and membership problems. Preserve enough structured information for the product’s recovery choices while keeping vendor-specific diagnostics at the appropriate adapter or operational boundary.

The sample’s revision-free store is intentionally small. Multi-record editing, optimistic conflicts, and cache freshness deserve explicit contracts like those in Repository.

Three tiers are not three classes per feature

A tiny local tool may co-locate these responsibilities with little ceremony. A larger application can enforce module boundaries and physical deployment separately. The number of files does not prove separation.

Avoid generic pass-through services that add a method for every table operation but own no policy. A use-case boundary should explain why an operation exists and which invariants it protects.

Trace one invariant through all three responsibilities

The loan duration rule belongs to the application or domain boundary because every presentation surface must obey it. The presenter parses a text field, but the service still validates the numeric range. A future command-line client or background job must not bypass the rule by skipping the original screen.

Inventory availability belongs to the authoritative storage operation at commit time. Checking availability in the service and decrementing it later would create a race: two callers could both observe the last copy before either records a loan.

The in-memory store keeps the check and mutation in one serialized operation. A database implementation needs an equivalent transaction or conditional update. The three-tier diagram identifies responsibilities; it does not create a database isolation level or make two separate calls atomic.

Dependency direction matters more than file count

Putting every type in a folder named Presentation, Business, or Data does not enforce the boundary. A presenter that opens the database directly still crosses it. A domain service returning a vendor-managed database object still exposes persistence lifecycle to its caller.

Use narrow protocols at the business boundary and return values meaningful to the use case. The data implementation adapts those operations to storage. The composition root supplies the implementation without making business rules depend on the concrete database library.

These logical layers may live in one process and one deployment. If the data tier moves across a network, latency, authentication, serialization, and uncertain outcomes become additional contracts. Distribution is an architectural decision with operational consequences, not a prerequisite for separating responsibilities in code.

Reliability requirements reveal missing boundaries

Suppose a successful loan must also send a notification. Sending before committing risks announcing a loan that fails. Sending afterward risks a crash leaving a committed loan without a notification. If reliable notification is required, record pending notification work durably with the loan where an atomic storage boundary permits it.

The sender then delivers that work with a retry and deduplication policy. This is a separate responsibility from the presenter showing a receipt. A simple three-tier sketch must be refined when the product requires reliable coordination of several effects.

Similarly, retries of a loan request need a stable operation identity if duplicate loans are possible. The service’s validation of days and inventory does not tell whether a repeated request is a retry or a genuinely new borrowing action.

Test business rules through the service with a recording store, storage invariants through the storage implementation, and presentation mapping with a fake service boundary. Integration tests then verify that the assembled tiers preserve those contracts together.

Exercise: add idempotent borrowing

Introduce a caller request ID stored atomically with the loan receipt. A repeated identical request should return the earlier receipt, while a conflicting payload under the same ID should be rejected. Simulate a lost response after commit and verify retry does not consume another copy.

Then replace the in-memory adapter with a fake that reports unavailable storage and confirm presentation shows the distinct unavailable state without changing loan-policy code.

Return to the Design Patterns roadmap.
entry.summary: Three-tier architecture separates presentation, application behavior, and data management. Those responsibilities can be deployed as client, application server, and database, while their source-code boundaries still need explicit dependency contracts. Merely creating three folders does not produce a useful architecture. The important question is which layer owns validation, domain decisions, persistence guarantees, and translation of failures.

entry.title: Merkle Trees in Swift: Commitments, Inclusion Proofs, and Canonical Encoding

link.title: Merkle Trees in Swift: Commitments, Inclusion Proofs, and Canonical Encoding

entry.content:
A Merkle tree commits to a collection through hashes of its leaves and internal nodes. An inclusion proof lets a verifier check one leaf using logarithmic sibling data rather than receiving the entire collection.

The security argument depends on more than calling SHA-256. Leaf encoding, internal-node encoding, ordering, tree shape, and the trusted root must all be specified.

These Swift 5.7 examples use CryptoKit, available before this article’s May 2025 date. The tree preserves leaf order, duplicates the final node at odd-width levels, and binds the original leaf count into the final commitment.

Separate leaves, parents, and the outer commitment

For payload x and child digests l, r, define:

\[L(x)=H(0x00\Vert x),\qquad P(l,r)=H(0x01\Vert l\Vert r).\]

Domain prefixes prevent the same bytes from being interpreted ambiguously as both a leaf and an internal node. The final root also includes a distinct prefix and a fixed-width big-endian leaf count.

import Foundation
import CryptoKit

func digest(_ data: Data) -> Data { Data(SHA256.hash(data: data)) }
func leafHash(_ payload: Data) -> Data { digest(Data([0]) + payload) }
func parentHash(_ left: Data, _ right: Data) -> Data { digest(Data([1]) + left + right) }
func committedRoot(_ treeRoot: Data, count: Int) -> Data {
    let encoded = Data((0..<8).map { offset in
        UInt8(truncatingIfNeeded: UInt64(count) >> (8 * (7 - offset)))
    })
    return digest(Data([3]) + encoded + treeRoot)
}

struct MerkleProof {
    let index: Int
    let leafCount: Int
    let siblings: [Data]
}

struct MerkleTree {
    private let levels: [[Data]]
    let leafCount: Int
    init(_ payloads: [Data]) {
        leafCount = payloads.count
        var built: [[Data]] = []
        if !payloads.isEmpty {
            built.append(payloads.map(leafHash))
            while built.last!.count > 1 {
                let current = built.last!
                var next: [Data] = []
                for index in stride(from: 0, to: current.count, by: 2) {
                    let right = index + 1 < current.count ? current[index + 1] : current[index]
                    next.append(parentHash(current[index], right))
                }
                built.append(next)
            }
        }
        levels = built
    }
    var root: Data {
        committedRoot(levels.last?.first ?? digest(Data([2])), count: leafCount)
    }
    func proof(at index: Int) -> MerkleProof? {
        guard (0..<leafCount).contains(index) else { return nil }
        var position = index
        var siblings: [Data] = []
        for level in levels.dropLast() {
            let sibling = position ^ 1
            siblings.append(level[sibling < level.count ? sibling : position])
            position /= 2
        }
        return MerkleProof(index: index, leafCount: leafCount, siblings: siblings)
    }
}

Without the outer count binding, duplicating the last node can make a three-leaf tree share a tree root with a four-leaf tree whose final leaf repeats the third. This format deliberately distinguishes those commitments.

Verify the expected shape as well as the hashes

func verify(payload: Data, proof: MerkleProof, root: Data) -> Bool {
    guard proof.leafCount > 0, (0..<proof.leafCount).contains(proof.index), root.count == 32 else {
        return false
    }
    var current = leafHash(payload)
    var index = proof.index
    var width = proof.leafCount
    var used = 0
    while width > 1 {
        guard used < proof.siblings.count else { return false }
        let sibling = proof.siblings[used]
        guard sibling.count == 32 else { return false }
        if index % 2 == 0 {
            if index + 1 == width && sibling != current { return false }
            current = parentHash(current, sibling)
        } else {
            current = parentHash(sibling, current)
        }
        index /= 2
        width = width / 2 + width % 2
        used += 1
    }
    guard used == proof.siblings.count else { return false }
    return committedRoot(current, count: proof.leafCount) == root
}

let payloads = ["A", "B", "C"].map { Data($0.utf8) }
let tree = MerkleTree(payloads)
let proof = tree.proof(at: 2)!
assert(verify(payload: payloads[2], proof: proof, root: tree.root))
assert(!verify(payload: Data("changed".utf8), proof: proof, root: tree.root))
assert(MerkleTree(payloads + [payloads[2]]).root != tree.root)
let extra = MerkleProof(index: 2, leafCount: 3, siblings: proof.siblings + [Data(repeating: 0, count: 32)])
assert(!verify(payload: payloads[2], proof: extra, root: tree.root))

Orientation follows the authenticated leaf position rather than untrusted left/right flags. Exact sibling count prevents accepting arbitrary extra proof material. The odd-node check enforces this format’s duplication rule.

The public helper assumes a nonnegative count when encoding a commitment. MerkleTree supplies array counts, and verification validates proof counts before calling it. A general serialization API should enforce those preconditions itself.

The root needs an authenticated origin

A proof establishes consistency with the supplied root. An attacker replacing both data and root can create a perfectly valid proof for different content.

Obtain roots from a trusted signature, authenticated channel, checkpoint, or another specified trust mechanism. A content hash is an integrity commitment, not an identity certificate by itself.

Likewise, the tree does not encrypt payloads. A public root or proof may support guessing attacks against a small known payload space; hashing alone does not hide predictable content.

Order and serialization define identity

Reordering leaves changes the commitment. If the domain treats records as an unordered set, canonicalize ordering by stable identifiers before building the tree and define duplicate handling.

Payload serialization must also be canonical. Equivalent dictionaries encoded in different key orders can produce different leaf hashes. Include type and schema information when distinct record formats could share the same raw byte representation.

This example is an application format, not a Bitcoin or certificate-transparency wire-format implementation. Those systems define their own tree shapes and proof semantics.

Account for bytes as well as nodes

Building hashes all payload bytes plus a linear number of fixed-size internal digests. Retaining all levels uses O(n) digests. An inclusion proof contains O(log n) siblings, and verification hashes that many parent pairs plus the payload.

For streaming construction, a frontier of partial subtree roots can reduce retained storage when proofs are not needed immediately. Serving arbitrary historical proofs requires additional storage or recomputation.

Update paths and append paths have different shape effects

Replacing one leaf in a fixed-size tree requires recalculating only its ancestors, giving logarithmic parent-hash work once the leaf position is known. The leaf’s own byte hashing still depends on payload size.

Appending changes the leaf count and can create new tree levels or alter odd-node duplication paths. The outer commitment must be recomputed even when part of the inner tree remains shared.

A persistent tree can retain historical roots while sharing unchanged subtrees. Keeping a root alone proves a commitment but does not guarantee the application retained enough data to serve every historical inclusion proof.

Membership does not prove completeness

An inclusion proof shows that one payload occupies a specified leaf position under the root. It does not show that the collection contains every event that should have been recorded, nor that no event was omitted before the root was created.

An audit system needs a protocol for sequencing, publication, and consistency between successive roots. A signed dishonest root still commits faithfully to the dishonest collection it describes.

Likewise, a proof of nonmembership requires another structure or ordering argument. Failure to provide an inclusion proof is not a cryptographic proof that a key is absent.

Make adversarial metadata part of the tests

let wrongIndex = MerkleProof(index: 1, leafCount: proof.leafCount, siblings: proof.siblings)
assert(!verify(payload: payloads[2], proof: wrongIndex, root: tree.root))
let wrongCount = MerkleProof(index: 2, leafCount: 4, siblings: proof.siblings)
assert(!verify(payload: payloads[2], proof: wrongCount, root: tree.root))
let singleton = MerkleTree([Data("one".utf8)])
assert(verify(payload: Data("one".utf8), proof: singleton.proof(at: 0)!, root: singleton.root))

These checks protect the format’s position and count commitments, not merely SHA-256 arithmetic. Keep them when refactoring proof transport or serialization.

Exercise: test the format as an adversarial boundary

Try wrong indices, altered counts, missing siblings, extra siblings, reordered siblings, and odd-width levels. Verify one-leaf trees with empty proofs and empty trees without inclusion proofs. Add serialized proof limits before decoding attacker-supplied arrays.

For the hashing API, see CryptoKit. Continue with Cryptographic Algorithms for the distinction between hashing, key agreement, and authentication.

Return to the Data Structures and Algorithms roadmap.

An inclusion proof lets a verifier check one leaf using logarithmic sibling data rather than receiving the entire collection. The security argument depends on more than calling SHA-256. Leaf encoding, internal-node encoding, ordering, tree shape, and the trusted root must all be specified.

entry.title: Front Controller in Swift: Validate and Dispatch Incoming Requests in One Place

link.title: Front Controller in Swift: Validate and Dispatch Incoming Requests in One Place

entry.content:
A front controller is a common entry point for incoming requests. It validates routing input, applies shared access policy, dispatches one use case, and maps outcomes into a consistent response model.

In an app, the request might come from a deep-link adapter, a command surface, or an internal navigation request. Central entry does not mean one object should contain every feature’s business logic.

These Swift 5.7 examples accept a small decoded request model with exact paths and parameters. A real URL or network adapter must handle decoding and duplicate query parameters before constructing this model.

Normalize input into a typed route before effects

enum UserRole { case reader, administrator }
struct RequestContext { let userID: Int?; let role: UserRole? }
struct IncomingRequest {
    let path: String
    let parameters: [String: String]
    let context: RequestContext
}
enum AppRoute {
    case book(Int)
    case search(String)
    case settings
    case administration
}
enum RouteFailure: Error { case unknown, malformed }

func parseRoute(_ request: IncomingRequest) throws -> AppRoute {
    switch request.path {
    case "/book":
        guard Set(request.parameters.keys) == ["id"],
              let text = request.parameters["id"], let id = Int(text), id > 0 else {
            throw RouteFailure.malformed
        }
        return .book(id)
    case "/search":
        guard Set(request.parameters.keys) == ["q"],
              let query = request.parameters["q"], (1...100).contains(query.count) else {
            throw RouteFailure.malformed
        }
        return .search(query)
    case "/settings":
        guard request.parameters.isEmpty else { throw RouteFailure.malformed }
        return .settings
    case "/admin":
        guard request.parameters.isEmpty else { throw RouteFailure.malformed }
        return .administration
    default:
        throw RouteFailure.unknown
    }
}

Typed routing prevents each downstream handler from independently parsing strings and inventing different defaults. Unsupported parameters are rejected rather than silently ignored.

This parser deliberately uses exact path matching. Case folding, percent decoding, trailing slashes, and canonicalization belong to the documented boundary adapter. Inconsistent normalization between routing and access checks can select different meanings for the same input.

Apply shared policy before dispatch

enum BookLookupFailure: Error { case missing, unavailable }
enum AppResponse: Equatable {
    case book(String)
    case results([String])
    case settings(String)
    case administration(String)
    case badRequest
    case notFound
    case signInRequired
    case forbidden
    case unavailable
}

struct FrontController {
    let loadBook: (Int) throws -> String
    let search: (String) throws -> [String]
    let settings: (Int) throws -> String
    let administration: () throws -> String

    func handle(_ request: IncomingRequest) -> AppResponse {
        let route: AppRoute
        do { route = try parseRoute(request) }
        catch RouteFailure.unknown { return .notFound }
        catch { return .badRequest }
        do {
            switch route {
            case let .book(id): return .book(try loadBook(id))
            case let .search(query): return .results(try search(query))
            case .settings:
                guard let userID = request.context.userID else { return .signInRequired }
                return .settings(try settings(userID))
            case .administration:
                guard request.context.userID != nil else { return .signInRequired }
                guard request.context.role == .administrator else { return .forbidden }
                return .administration(try administration())
            }
        } catch BookLookupFailure.missing {
            return .notFound
        } catch {
            return .unavailable
        }
    }
}

The context is a trusted application snapshot, not a role accepted from arbitrary query parameters. In a server deployment, backend authorization still needs to enforce access independently of client navigation.

Book pages and search are public under this example policy, while settings and administration have different access requirements. A product can choose another policy, but it should be visible in one coherent place.

Test that denied requests do not reach effects

var administrationCalls = 0
let controller = FrontController(
    loadBook: { id in
        guard id == 7 else { throw BookLookupFailure.missing }
        return "Swift"
    },
    search: { [$0] },
    settings: { "Settings for \($0)" },
    administration: { administrationCalls += 1; return "Administration" }
)
let anonymous = RequestContext(userID: nil, role: nil)
let reader = RequestContext(userID: 1, role: .reader)
let administrator = RequestContext(userID: 2, role: .administrator)
assert(controller.handle(IncomingRequest(path: "/book", parameters: ["id": "7"], context: anonymous)) == .book("Swift"))
assert(controller.handle(IncomingRequest(path: "/book", parameters: ["id": "bad"], context: anonymous)) == .badRequest)
assert(controller.handle(IncomingRequest(path: "/admin", parameters: [:], context: reader)) == .forbidden)
assert(administrationCalls == 0)
assert(controller.handle(IncomingRequest(path: "/admin", parameters: [:], context: administrator)) == .administration("Administration"))
assert(administrationCalls == 1)

An invalid ID is rejected before lookup. A forbidden administration request cannot invoke the administration capability. A missing book and unavailable storage remain distinct responses.

The effect closures keep the example testable. A network-backed capability should expose asynchronous behavior instead of blocking this synchronous interface.

flowchart LR
    accTitle: A front controller validates and authorizes before selecting a use case
    Input[Decoded request] --> Parse[Typed route parsing]
    Parse --> Policy[Shared access policy]
    Policy --> Dispatch[Dispatch one use case]
    Dispatch --> Outcome[Map domain outcome]
    Outcome --> Response[Application response]

Keep request scope coherent

Read account and role facts once for the request rather than consulting a mutable global session between validation and dispatch. If authorization can change during long asynchronous work, the effect boundary needs an appropriate revalidation or server-enforced policy.

Request identity also helps diagnostics and idempotency. A common entry point can attach a correlation ID, but an ID alone does not deduplicate external writes.

The dictionary parameter model cannot represent duplicate keys. A real decoder must reject duplicates or apply a documented policy before using it. Converting to a dictionary too early can discard input distinctions that validation needed.

Front Controller is not every coordinator

A coordinator owns navigation and child-flow lifetime. A front controller owns incoming-request admission and dispatch. It can delegate a validated route to a coordinator rather than manipulating all screen objects itself.

A mediator coordinates ongoing colleague interactions. A chain of responsibility can implement extensible dispatch stages inside a front controller, but its ordering and terminal rejection semantics remain important.

A facade exposes a coherent use case. Several route handlers can call the same facade while the front controller remains responsible only for entry policy and result mapping.

Avoid the central switch becoming the whole application

A closed route enum and switch are clear for a small domain. A large plugin host may need a registry of typed handlers with explicit conflict and access policies.

Do not replace a readable switch with runtime discovery solely to avoid editing one file. Conversely, do not keep adding business rules and infrastructure adapters into one controller until every feature depends on it.

Keep shared admission logic central and feature-specific work behind narrow capabilities. That gives new routes an obvious assembly home without turning the entry point into a service locator.

Canonicalize once at the transport boundary

The example deliberately receives an already decoded request. A real URL entry point must first define percent-decoding, path normalization, repeated query parameters, and maximum input size. Decoding twice can turn an apparently literal value into a separator or another reserved character.

Use one transport adapter to produce the IncomingRequest representation, then parse routes from that representation. Do not let each handler apply its own decoding rules. Exact route matching is useful only when every handler agrees on what the path and parameter values mean.

Repeated parameters also need a policy. If the URL contains two book IDs, choosing the first in one layer and the last in another can lead to a decision about one entity followed by an effect on another. Reject ambiguity or normalize it consistently before authorization and dispatch.

Authentication context must come from a trusted source

A user-controlled query parameter saying role=admin is not authorization context. The request context supplied here represents a result already established by the trusted entry adapter or session system.

The front controller checks access before dispatching a protected handler, but the domain service must still enforce permissions relevant to the specific operation. A route-level role check cannot establish ownership of every requested book or protect an operation invoked through another entry point.

Keep malformed input distinct from denied access and missing resources according to the application’s disclosure policy. Some services intentionally conceal whether a protected resource exists. That policy should be consistent across entry points, rather than an accidental consequence of handler order.

One entry point need not become one enormous switch

A front controller centralizes the common request lifecycle: decode, parse, apply shared policy, dispatch, and map outcomes. It can delegate route-specific work to small handlers. A growing switch containing database queries, UI creation, billing logic, and retries no longer provides a useful boundary.

Keep parsing pure where possible. A parser test can then enumerate paths and parameter cases without constructing every downstream dependency. Handler tests focus on domain outcomes, while front-controller tests verify that denied requests produce no effects and errors map to the promised response.

For asynchronous handlers, preserve cancellation and distinguish a timed-out response from a known failed effect. A request may have committed remotely before the caller stopped waiting. Retrying a mutating route needs an idempotency policy or reconciliation mechanism; centralized dispatch does not supply one.

Finally, tracing should record the normalized route and outcome while redacting credentials and sensitive parameters. A convenient central logging point can otherwise become a convenient central data leak.

Exercise: add an asynchronous publish route

Parse a request ID and draft identity, enforce its required account policy, and call a publishing facade. Map complete, pending-index, invalid input, and unavailable outcomes distinctly. Test duplicate requests and cancellation without assuming that a cancelled client call means no remote commit occurred.

Return to the Design Patterns roadmap.

Central entry does not mean one object should contain every feature’s business logic.
